sources.title: Scientific Revolutions (Fall 2012 archive edition)

say.text: Welcome to class 40. Last class, Europe's churches split apart. Today, people change how they study nature itself.

show.text: The Scientific Revolution

say.text: Historians use the name 'Scientific Revolution' for a stretch of change in Europe. It is often dated from 1543 to 1687.

show.text: Scientific Revolution: about 1543 to 1687 (dates are debated)

say.text: First, the old picture. Ptolemy's model said Earth sits still at the centre of the heavens.

show.text: Ptolemy's model: Earth stands still at the centre

ask.q: In the old Ptolemy picture, what sits still at the centre?
ask.why: Ptolemy's model described the cosmos with Earth stationary at the centre.

say.text: Then Nicolaus Copernicus argued the opposite. Earth is a planet, and the planets circle the Sun. This is called heliocentric, or Sun-centred.

show.text: A simple diagram: the Sun in the middle, with Earth and the other planets travelling around it.

ask.q: In Copernicus's idea, what circles the Sun?
ask.why: Copernicus concluded that Earth is a planet and that all the planets circle the Sun.

say.text: He could not prove it. But his arguments were strong enough to turn the tide of thinking. Proof would need better measuring and new tools.

show.text: A strong argument, not yet a proof

say.text: Next, Johannes Kepler asked what shape the orbits are. After about 20 years of work, he found they are ellipses, not circles.

show.text: A circle stretched into an oval, with the Sun placed off-centre at one of two special points inside it.

ask.q: What shape did Kepler find for a planet's orbit?
ask.why: Kepler's first law says planets move on elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.

say.text: Now the telescope. On 7 January 1610, Galileo aimed his homemade 20-power telescope at Jupiter.

show.text: Galileo at a window at night, looking through a long thin telescope at a bright Jupiter with tiny dots beside it.

say.text: He saw small lights beside Jupiter. They moved from night to night. By 15 January he decided they were moons.

ask.q: What did Galileo decide the little lights near Jupiter were?
ask.why: He watched them over several nights and concluded they were moons going around Jupiter.

say.text: Why does that matter? It showed that not everything circles Earth. That was strong evidence for Copernicus.

show.text: Not everything circles Earth

say.text: He saw more. The Moon had mountains and craters. It was not the smooth, perfect ball that the old teaching claimed.

show.text: A telescope view of the Moon with a rough edge, craters and long mountain shadows.

say.text: Late in 1610 he watched Venus. It showed phases, like our Moon. That tells us Venus circles the Sun.

show.text: Venus shown in a row: a small round disk, then larger crescents.

ask.q: What did Venus showing phases tell Galileo?
wrong: Venus has no light of its own and is not a planet
ask.why: The order of the phases showed that Venus goes around the Sun. This contradicted the Ptolemaic picture.

say.text: Galileo also pushed a habit. Do experiments, measure carefully, and ask nature itself.

show.text: Experiment: ask nature, then measure

ask.q: What did Galileo urge scientists to do?
ask.right: Make observations and experiments and measure carefully
wrong: Trust ancient writers instead of looking
ask.why: He advocated experiments and observations, using careful measurements, to find out how nature works.

say.text: Soon scientists organised around this habit. In 1660 the Royal Society began in London. Its motto means 'take nobody's word for it'.

show.text: Nullius in verba: 'Take nobody's word for it.'

ask.q: What does the Royal Society's motto, Nullius in verba, mean?
ask.why: The Society's aim was to promote experiments and argument, not to rely on authority alone.

say.text: The microscope opened a second hidden world. In 1665 Robert Hooke published Micrographia. It is full of engraved drawings of things seen through his microscope.

show.text: A page from Micrographia: a huge, finely engraved drawing of a flea.

say.text: Hooke looked at thin slices of cork and saw tiny pores. He called them cells. Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscopes then showed blood cells and more.

show.text: How much early instruments magnified

ask.q: Hooke looked at thin slices of which material and gave us the word 'cell'?
ask.why: Looking at thin slices of cork, Hooke described tiny pores. He coined the word 'cell' while studying plant structure.

say.text: Now the big finish. In 1687 Isaac Newton published the Principia. It set out three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation.

show.text: Principia, 1687: laws of motion and gravity

say.text: Take the first law. A thing keeps still, or keeps moving in a straight line, unless a force acts on it. Think of a puck gliding on ice.

show.text: First law: no force, no change of motion

ask.q: By Newton's first law, a moving object keeps moving in a straight line unless what happens?
wrong: It reaches the end of the day
ask.why: The first law, the law of inertia, says an object keeps its motion unless an outside force changes it.

say.text: Then gravity. Every object pulls on every other object. And the same rules work in the sky and on the ground.

show.text: One set of rules for Earth and sky

ask.q: What was new about Newton's gravity?
ask.right: One set of rules applied to both the heavens and the Earth
wrong: It only worked for the planets
It was never written in numbers
ask.why: Newton's laws were a united set of principles that applied to the heavens and the Earth in the same way.

say.text: A small joke. The famous apple is never mentioned in the Principia. It is a story that grew later.

show.text: A cartoon apple with a question mark above it.

say.text: Look how long this took. From Copernicus's book in 1543 to Newton's Principia is 144 years. That is more than a century.

show.text: Years since Copernicus's book (1543)

ask.q: About how many years passed between Copernicus's book (1543) and Newton's Principia (1687)?
ask.why: 1687 minus 1543 is 144, which the chart shows.

say.text: Europe did not do this alone. Ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra around 965. He wrote his Book of Optics in Cairo, under house arrest, between 1010 and 1021.

show.text: Ibn al-Haytham: Book of Optics

ask.q: Where did Ibn al-Haytham write his Book of Optics?
ask.right: In Cairo, while under house arrest
ask.why: He wrote it in Cairo during eleven years of house arrest, 1010 to 1021.

say.text: His book used repeated, controlled testing. Its Latin version reached Europe around 1200. It stayed the top optics book until Kepler's work of 1604.

show.text: Ibn al-Haytham's method: test, repeat, check. Translated into Latin. Studied for centuries in Europe.

say.text: Astronomers at the Maragha observatory in Persia, led by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, built the Tusi couple. It is a small circle turning inside a larger one.

show.text: A small circle rolling inside a larger circle that is twice its size.

say.text: Some of Copernicus's maths was nearly identical to the Tusi couple. But the Maragha scholars had no Sun-centred model.

show.text: Maragha: new maths for the planets, Earth still at the centre | Copernicus: used similar maths, put the Sun at the centre

ask.q: What did the Maragha scholars not have?
ask.why: The Maragha scholars improved Ptolemy's models, but they did not have a heliocentric model.

say.text: Now science and religion. Galileo was a devout Catholic. In 1616 Church advisers judged heliocentrism false and heretical. He was warned not to hold or defend it.

show.text: 1616: the warning

say.text: In 1632 he published the Dialogue, and a trial followed in 1633. He was found guilty of 'strong suspicion of heresy'. He lived under house arrest for the rest of his life.

show.text: 1633: guilty of strong suspicion of heresy

ask.q: What was Galileo found guilty of in 1633?
ask.why: He was convicted of strong suspicion of heresy, a lesser charge than heresy itself.

say.text: The story is not simply science against religion. In 1616, much of the scientific evidence did not yet clearly favour a moving Earth. The trial turned on whether he broke the Church's order.

show.text: Common story: science versus religion | Historians add: personal quarrels, politics, and what counted as proof

ask.q: Why do historians warn against the simple 'science versus religion' story of Galileo?
ask.right: The real events involved evidence, politics, personalities and an order he was accused of breaking
wrong: The Church had no part in it
ask.why: Sources describe a mix of disputed evidence, a Church order and personal conflicts. It was more than a simple clash.

say.text: So was it a 'revolution'? A famous historian opened his book with a surprising line.

show.text: 'There was no such thing as the Scientific Revolution, and this is a book about it.' (Steven Shapin, 1996)

say.text: His point is that change was slower and messier than one event. There was real continuity with the medieval past. Yet most agree the pace of change picked up.

show.text: Slow, not sudden | Linked to the medieval past | Still, the pace clearly sped up

ask.q: Many historians now see the Scientific Revolution as what?
ask.right: A long, messy period of change, not a single event
wrong: A single event on one day
ask.why: Many historians treat it as a topic area. Most agree the pace of change increased.

say.text: Here is the frame of reference. Galileo was born in 1564, the same year as Shakespeare. He died in 1642, the year Newton was born.

show.text: 1564 Galileo and Shakespeare born | 1603 Tokugawa shogunate begins in Japan | 1610 Starry Messenger | 1618 Thirty Years' War begins | 1620 Mayflower lands | 1632 Taj Mahal begun | 1633 Galileo's trial | 1642 Galileo dies, Newton born | 1660 Royal Society founded | 1687 Principia

ask.q: Which of these people was born in the same year as Galileo, 1564?
ask.why: Galileo and Shakespeare were both born in 1564. Newton was born in 1642, Kepler in 1571 and Copernicus in 1473.

say.text: To sum up. People tested ideas with telescopes, microscopes and experiments, shared the results, and let others check them.

show.text: Copernicus: Sun-centred idea | Kepler: elliptical orbits | Galileo: telescope and experiments | Newton: one set of laws | Many cultures contributed

ask.q: Which sentence best sums up the new way of studying nature?
ask.right: Test ideas with observation, measurement and experiment, and share results so others can check them
wrong: Believe the oldest books without question
Use thinking only and never look
ask.why: The Royal Society's motto and Galileo's habit of measuring both point to testing ideas against evidence.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Galileo and the playwright William Shakespeare were both born this year.
Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in Japan, starting nearly three centuries of Tokugawa rule.
The Thirty Years' War began in Europe. Kepler's last law of planetary motion is dated to about the same time.
The Mayflower brought Pilgrims to Plymouth. Francis Bacon's Novum Organum also appeared.
Galileo's Dialogue appeared in 1632. Shah Jahan began building the Taj Mahal in India, and Galileo went to Rome for trial in 1633.
Galileo died, and Isaac Newton was born in the same year.
The Royal Society was founded in London. Charles II was crowned king of England and Louis XIV began his personal rule in France.
Hooke's Micrographia was published, and the Royal Society began its journal Philosophical Transactions.

other_side.claim: The Scientific Revolution was a single great turning point in how people studied nature.
other_side.other_view: Many historians now doubt there was one coherent event. Shapin opened a famous book by saying so, and he stressed continuity with medieval thought. Copernicus was cautious, and few people paid attention to his work for about fifty years. Most scholars still agree change sped up, and some argue the idea remains a useful category.

other_side.claim: Copernicus's mathematics owed a great deal to the astronomers of Maragha.
other_side.other_view: Some scholars say Copernicus could not have reached his model without them, because his diagrams and maths closely match Tusi's. Others find no evidence the Maragha scholars influenced his Sun-centred system. They note that he never mentioned al-Tusi or Ibn al-Shatir, and that these scholars had no Sun-centred model.

other_side.claim: Galileo's trial shows science fighting religion.
other_side.other_view: The Church's condemnation became the iconic illustration of conflict between science and religion. Some historians say that is too simple. They point to a Church order, personal quarrels, politics, and the view that the evidence was not yet decisive.

other_side.claim: Galileo's telescope settled whether Earth moves.
other_side.other_view: The phases of Venus contradicted Ptolemy's model but also fit a rival Sun-and-planets model. Defenders of the Church's position argue that the evidence in 1616 was not firmly on the side of heliocentrism.

other_side.claim: The Scientific Revolution was mainly a European story.
other_side.other_view: One recent preprint argues that Islamic astronomy was an independent scientific revolution, not just a bridge between Greece and Europe. This is a newer view and not everyone shares it.
